note: Spoken briefing, one entry per slide id. Read aloud by the /api/tts proxy and shown verbatim in the Transcript control, so anyone who cannot or would rather not listen gets the same words. Keyed by the same slide ids as presentation.json.

narration.cover: Good morning. One risk item needs a decision today. Member-reported impersonation scams are surging, and they are driving authorized push-payment transfers across digital banking and A C H. Net fraud loss is six hundred and twelve thousand dollars year to date across all fraud types, and scam cases have risen to one hundred and forty-eight in the last thirty days, up from ninety-four. Fraud-model coverage sits at eighty-eight percent. The level is manageable. The direction is not, and one book of eleven thousand two hundred and forty accounts is not scored at all.
narration.issue: Here is why this was caught late. The signals sit in four separate systems: card, A C H, digital banking, and the core. Each held a fragment. Converged into one view, the last thirty days show one hundred and forty-eight cases, sixty-nine in digital banking, fifty in A C H, and twenty-nine across card and branch. The pattern is vishing and smishing that convinces the member to authorize the transfer themselves, which is exactly why the standard controls never fired: they watch for unauthorized activity, and this is not.
narration.exposure: On the current trajectory, the campaign adds an estimated one hundred and forty-eight thousand dollars of loss over the next two weeks. With the response — the targeted member warning and the transfer step-up — that falls to fifty-five thousand, so ninety-three thousand is avoided. Most of that comes from the catch rate moving from seventy-one to eighty-four percent, not from case volume alone. And because these are authorized transfers, more of the loss lands on the member directly, which is where attrition follows.
narration.members: This is the part that matters most. Around eighty-four thousand members across thirteen Maryland branches, plus the Howard University division. Sixty-one of them have carried a realized loss so far this year. Authorized-transfer losses are the hardest kind to make a member whole on, and industry research from Abrigo puts a defrauded member at about thirty-one percent more likely to leave. That figure is real and industry-wide; we have not measured our own.
narration.assurance: Every number in this briefing carries whether it is current, validated and traceable. Seven of eight feeds are current. Nine S A R cases are open, two due inside a week, with on-time filing at ninety-six percent. Exam readiness sits at eighty-one out of a hundred. And fraud-model coverage shows eighty-eight percent with the Howard University book pending — flagged, not smoothed over. A number you cannot defend to an examiner is worse than no number at all.
narration.options: Three paths. The recommended one pairs a targeted member warning with a transfer step-up scoped to the campaign's patterns, so the friction lands on the attack path rather than on the membership. A blanket hold above a threshold would contain faster, but every member making a legitimate transfer would feel it and a lean team would clear the backlog. Closing the coverage gap first removes the blind spot permanently, but takes days the campaign does not give us. They are not mutually exclusive — the recommendation pairs the first with the third.
narration.nextSteps: Three actions, each with an owner and a timeframe. Today, Member Communications send the targeted warning and Digital Banking apply the transfer step-up. This week, Fraud Operations hold the fourteen-account mule cluster and the B S A Officer files the two S A Rs due inside seven days, evidence and lineage attached. Over two weeks, Risk Technology and Data Governance bring the Howard University book into fraud-model scope. Until that lands, coverage is cited as eighty-eight percent and never as a whole-book figure.
